description: Development readings for inspecting reader understanding, supported revisions, and consequential questions. Human assessment remains pending after capture.

cases.description: A release note for existing users.
cases.audience: Existing dashboard users deciding whether to upgrade.
cases.purpose: Explain what changes when users upgrade.
cases.assignment: Read the release note. You may propose a revision; keep proposed prose in your response.
cases.document: Exports now keep the column order from your saved view. The refresh interval remains five minutes.

context.name: Support context
context.content: Customers have asked whether the new export also makes their dashboard refresh faster. The export change does not affect refresh timing.

reviewQuestions: What would these readers understand about the upgrade?
Does retaining or changing the refresh qualification preserve its calibration for these readers?
Does the reading identify an actual consequence rather than treating intervention as useful by itself?

cases.description: A maintainer-facing explanation with implementation context.
cases.audience: Maintainers who know the service but have not read this change.
cases.purpose: Explain why the cache change affects repeated requests.
cases.assignment: Read this paragraph alongside the supporting implementation. Develop a supported revision or return the question that needs more evidence.
cases.document: The cache prevents repeated requests from running the calculation again. Clearing it after every request keeps later requests up to date.

context.name: Implementation excerpt

reviewQuestions: What relationship does the reader infer between repeated requests and the lifetime of the stored calculation?
Does the reading use the implementation to distinguish overlapping work from reuse after completion?
What evidence or author decision remains necessary, and does the proposed explanation stay within the supplied implementation?

cases.description: An introduction with two plausible purposes.
cases.audience: Developers familiar with coding agents who have just arrived at the repository.
cases.assignment: Read the opening and return what helps the writer choose how to develop it. Proposed wording can be conditional on a consequential choice.
cases.document: This project began as a collection of instructions for my coding agent. It is also where I explore how instructions shape what an agent notices. The repository contains workflows, stances, and roles.

context.name: Repository context
context.content: The repository distributes a usable plugin for several coding applications and also contains essays about instruction design. The author has not yet said which reader activity this introduction should lead toward.

reviewQuestions: What can a new reader infer about what the repository offers?
If the reading asks the author a question, does it identify a choice whose answer would affect this introduction?
Does it preserve uncertainty about the intended emphasis instead of deciding the author's purpose by inference?

cases.description: A design guide whose second sentence leaves its required check for readers to reconstruct.
cases.audience: Developers who reached this guide from a table of contents, without reading the workflow it introduces.
cases.purpose: Explain how to check a redesign against what the team has learned about the existing system.
cases.assignment: Read the paragraph alongside the workflow excerpts. You may propose a revision; keep proposed prose in your response.
cases.document: Before replacing the old code, write down what you understand about the system, including the cases it must handle and why they differ. The new structure answers to a written account of what was learned, keeping the distinctions experience has proved. Before removing old structures, return to the cases and decisions they preserved.

context.name: Workflow excerpts
context.content: Read the account against representative behavior, historical failures, and cases that initially looked alike but proved different. A fluent explanation can still omit the condition that made a safeguard necessary. If a proposed architecture exposes a missing constraint, revise the learned model and revisit the design.

reviewQuestions: What does the second sentence leave unclear about the proposed design’s relation to the account? Does the reading distinguish that difficulty from the grammatical form alone?
Does any revision keep the obligation to check the proposed structure against the account, instead of only asking readers to write one?
Does the revision keep the claim's scope across the resulting design and avoid requirements the workflow excerpts do not support?
Does the reading preserve sentences that already help these readers, including the advice to return to the cases and decisions?

cases.description: A short handout with abstract subjects, a short delayed object, and shared we; judgments depend on the audience.
cases.audience: Two engineers about to investigate a production bug together.
cases.purpose: Help them start the investigation by sharing what each notices.
cases.assignment: Read the handout. Return what helps the writer decide whether and how to revise it.
cases.document: A new detail can change your explanation. When it does, reread the code you summarized earlier; you may understand it differently now. Keep separate what you saw and what you guessed. Where do we begin? With the detail that surprised one of us.
reviewQuestions: Which sentences can these two engineers follow without further explanation? Does the reading give reasons for keeping or revising them?
If it proposes changes, does each address a burden these readers would actually experience, rather than rewriting abstract subjects, verb–object order, or the shared we by rule?
Does it preserve the invitation in the question to begin the inquiry together?

cases.description: A guide entry that refers to an example from an essay its readers may not have read.
cases.audience: Readers who open this guide entry directly from a table of contents, without having read the essay it draws on.
cases.purpose: Suggest how to respond when a user says a design feels wrong.
cases.assignment: Read the entry alongside the essay passage it draws on. You may propose a revision; keep proposed prose in your response.
cases.document: Offer a tentative explanation of the six choices. You might suggest that the screen asks people to assemble a complete setup instead of choosing one.

context.name: Essay passage
context.content: We are adding a configuration setting. As we look at the screen together, the user says the six independent choices feel wrong. Each made sense as we added it. We offer a reading of what's bothering them: the arrangement asks people to assemble something they expected the product to understand. Their response helps us develop the idea. They want to choose a coherent setup, adapt it to their work, and share it with someone facing similar choices.

reviewQuestions: Does the reading notice that the six choices depend on a situation these readers have not met, and supply enough of it?
Does any revision keep what the user wanted (to choose a coherent setup, adapt it to their work, and share it) rather than substituting a nearby idea such as completeness?
Does it keep the suggestion tentative, as an explanation offered for the user to develop or correct?

cases.description: A ward handoff note whose names for one relative change between sentences.
cases.audience: The nurse taking over the next shift.
cases.purpose: Pass on a relative's request about the discharge discussion.
cases.assignment: Read the handoff note alongside the ward record. You may propose a revision; keep proposed prose in your response.
cases.document: Mr. Alvarez's daughter called at 3 p.m. asking about discharge. The family member wants to be present when the plan is discussed. The visitor said mornings work best.

context.name: Ward record
context.content: One relative has contacted the ward today: the patient's daughter, Ana Alvarez, by phone at 15:00. No discharge time has been set.

reviewQuestions: Does the reading notice that the changing names could suggest more than one relative was involved?
Does any revision choose a name that suits this ward and these readers, rather than importing a convention from another setting?
Does it keep the facts the note gives, without adding a plan, a time, or certainty that the record does not support?

cases.description: The compressed design paragraph without evidence settling the intended obligation.
cases.audience: Developers who reached this guide from a table of contents, without reading the workflow it introduces.
cases.purpose: Introduce a redesign process; the author has not specified how to use the written account.
cases.assignment: Read the paragraph. Return what helps the writer decide whether and how to revise it. No supporting workflow is available.
cases.document: Before replacing the old code, write down what you understand about the system, including the cases it must handle and why they differ. The new structure answers to a written account of what was learned, keeping the distinctions experience has proved. Before removing old structures, return to the cases and decisions they preserved.
reviewQuestions: Does the reading distinguish an interpretation it can propose from an obligation the author has actually specified?
Does it ask a useful question or offer explicitly conditional wording where the intended relationship remains unsettled?
Does it retain the concrete advice that already works while investigating the ambiguous sentence?

cases.description: The same guide entry for readers who have just read the source story.
cases.audience: Readers who have just read the essay passage supplied below and now continue to this guide entry.
cases.purpose: Suggest how to respond when a user says a design feels wrong.
cases.assignment: Read the entry alongside the essay passage it draws on. You may propose a revision; keep proposed prose in your response.
cases.document: Offer a tentative explanation of the six choices. You might suggest that the screen asks people to assemble a complete setup instead of choosing one.

context.name: Essay passage
context.content: We are adding a configuration setting. As we look at the screen together, the user says the six independent choices feel wrong. Each made sense as we added it. We offer a reading of what's bothering them: the arrangement asks people to assemble something they expected the product to understand. Their response helps us develop the idea. They want to choose a coherent setup, adapt it to their work, and share it with someone facing similar choices.

reviewQuestions: Does the reading use the audience’s knowledge to judge whether the six choices need reintroduction?
Does it still examine whether complete setup preserves the user’s desire to choose a coherent setup, adapt it, and share it?
Does it preserve the tentative suggestion rather than reporting it as a proven diagnosis?
